Question 1: Boundary and margin

Use margin-geometry-20.csv from the combined ZIP, which contains 20 observations with predictors x1,x2x_1,x_2 and class labels y∈{−1,1}y\in\{-1,1\}. Consider the score

f(x)=0.8x1+0.6x2. f(x)=0.8x_1+0.6x_2.

Since ∥(0.8,0.6)∥2=1\|(0.8,0.6)\|_2=1, the lines f(x)=±1f(x)=\pm1 are each a distance 1 from the decision boundary f(x)=0f(x)=0.

  1. Calculate the distance from every observation to the decision boundary and its functional margin yf(x)yf(x). In a table, report these values and whether each observation is inside, on, or beyond the margin for its class. Compare yf(x)yf(x) with 1 to make this distinction.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

data = pd.read_csv("data/margin-geometry-20.csv")
data["f(x)"] = 0.8 * data["x1"] + 0.6 * data["x2"]
data["distance"] = data["f(x)"].abs()
data["yf(x)"] = data["y"] * data["f(x)"]
on_margin = np.isclose(data["yf(x)"], 1, atol=1e-9, rtol=0)
data["position"] = np.where(
    on_margin, "on", np.where(data["yf(x)"] < 1, "inside", "beyond")
)

print(data[["observation", "x1", "x2", "y", "f(x)", "distance",
            "yf(x)", "position"]].round(4).to_string(index=False))

  1. Plot the observations, the boundary f(x)=0f(x)=0, and the margin lines f(x)=±1f(x)=\pm1. Distinguish the two classes and identify the observations inside the margin in your plot.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))
for label, color, marker in [(1, "tab:blue", "o"), (-1, "tab:orange", "^")]:
    group = data[data["y"] == label]
    ax.scatter(group["x1"], group["x2"], color=color, marker=marker,
               s=60, label=f"y = {label}")

inside = data[data["position"] == "inside"]
ax.scatter(inside["x1"], inside["x2"], s=180, facecolors="none",
           edgecolors="red", linewidths=1.5, label="Inside class margin")
for row in data.itertuples(index=False):
    ax.annotate(str(row.observation), (row.x1, row.x2),
                xytext=(5, 5), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9)

x1 = np.linspace(-3.2, 3.2, 200)
for level, style in [(0, "-"), (1, "--"), (-1, "--")]:
    ax.plot(x1, (level - 0.8 * x1) / 0.6, color="black",
            linestyle=style, label=f"f(x) = {level}")

ax.set(xlim=(-3.2, 3.2), ylim=(-3, 3), xlabel="$x_1$", ylabel="$x_2$")
ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("Misclassified observations:",
      data.loc[data["yf(x)"] < 0, "observation"].tolist())

Question 2: Margin in four dimensions

Use margin-geometry-4d.csv from the combined ZIP, which contains 50 observations with four predictors and class labels y∈{−1,1}y\in\{-1,1\}. Consider the linear score

f(𝒙)=β0+𝒙𝖳𝜷,β0=−1,𝜷=(1,2,−2,4)𝖳. f(\mathbf{x})=\beta_0+\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \qquad \beta_0=-1, \quad \boldsymbol{\beta}=(1,2,-2,4)^{\mathsf T}.

  1. Project the observations onto the direction of 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta} and plot their positions on one axis. Distinguish the two classes and mark the decision boundary. Use the plot to calculate the geometric margin MM, the distance from the boundary to the closest observation.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

data4 = pd.read_csv("data/margin-geometry-4d.csv")
X4 = data4[["x1", "x2", "x3", "x4"]].to_numpy()
beta = np.array([1, 2, -2, 4])
beta0 = -1
beta_norm = np.linalg.norm(beta)
boundary = -beta0 / beta_norm
data4["projection"] = X4 @ (beta / beta_norm)
data4["f(x)"] = beta0 + X4 @ beta
data4["distance"] = np.abs(data4["projection"] - boundary)
M = data4["distance"].min()
closest = data4[np.isclose(data4["distance"], M, atol=1e-9, rtol=0)]

print(data4[["observation", "y", "projection", "f(x)", "distance"]]
      .round(4).to_string(index=False))
print(f"Geometric margin M = {M:.4f}")
print("Closest observations:", closest["observation"].tolist())

left = min(data4["projection"].min(), boundary) - 0.3
right = max(data4["projection"].max(), boundary) + 0.3
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3))
ax.axvspan(left, boundary, color="tab:orange", alpha=0.12)
ax.axvspan(boundary, right, color="tab:blue", alpha=0.12)
ax.axhline(0, color="gray", linewidth=0.8)
for label, color, marker in [(1, "tab:blue", "o"), (-1, "tab:orange", "^")]:
    group = data4[data4["y"] == label]
    ax.scatter(group["projection"], np.zeros(len(group)), color=color,
               marker=marker, s=60, alpha=0.8, label=f"y = {label}", zorder=3)

ax.axvline(boundary, color="black", linestyle="--", label="f(x) = 0")
ax.scatter(closest["projection"], np.zeros(len(closest)), s=180,
           facecolors="none", edgecolors="red", label="Closest", zorder=4)
for label in [-1, 1]:
    group = closest[closest["y"] == label]
    if not group.empty:
        ids = ", ".join(group["observation"].astype(str))
        ax.annotate(f"Observations {ids}", (group["projection"].mean(), 0),
                    xytext=(0, 20), textcoords="offset points", ha="center")
nearest = closest.iloc[0]
ax.annotate("", (boundary, -0.15), (nearest["projection"], -0.15),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="|-|", color="red"))
ax.text((boundary + nearest["projection"]) / 2, -0.25,
        f"M = {M:.4f}", ha="center", color="red")
ax.text((left + boundary) / 2, 0.32, "f(x) < 0", ha="center")
ax.text((boundary + right) / 2, 0.32, "f(x) > 0", ha="center")
ax.set(xlim=(left, right), ylim=(-0.4, 0.65), yticks=[],
       xlabel=r"Projection $t = \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\beta}/\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|$")
ax.legend(loc="upper center", ncol=4, fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The geometric margin is 1.

  1. Express the same decision boundary using the SVM normalization in which the smallest functional margin yif(𝒙i)y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i) is set to 1. What are the corresponding values of 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta} and β0\beta_0?

The smallest functional margin is m=min⁡iyif(𝒙i)=5m=\min_i y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i)=5. Dividing both the intercept and all coefficients by mm gives

β̃0=−15=−0.2,𝜷̃=15(1,2,−2,4)𝖳=(0.2,0.4,−0.4,0.8)𝖳. \widetilde{\beta}_0=-\frac15=-0.2, \qquad \widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}} =\frac15(1,2,-2,4)^{\mathsf T} =(0.2,0.4,-0.4,0.8)^{\mathsf T}.

Question 3: Peer review of a Homework 7 skill

The instructor’s GitHub account, rqzhu-aide, will open a GitHub Issue in the repository containing your Homework 7 submission. It will link to one assigned student’s repository.

  1. Use the skill. Find the complete skill definition in the assigned student’s Homework 7 report. Copy it without changes into a local SKILL.md file in your own folder. You do not need to install it. Give your agent the path to the file and explicitly ask it to follow that skill while analyzing the SAheart data, using the response and predictor coding from Homework 7. Provide the necessary data information, but no additional preferences about methods, figures, model selection, or report style. Let the skill direct the analysis.

    Monitor the time, your token use, and your weekly quota while the agent works. If the run is taking too long or using your allowance too quickly, you may send a steer message asking the agent to finish immediately, or stop the run and summarize what you observed. A steer message redirects an agent while it is working; learn how to send one in your AI tool before starting.

  2. Write a peer review. Read the student’s submitted report and what the skill produced in your run. Give a brief overall assessment, followed by three major items the author could improve. You may comment on any aspect of the skill or report. For each item, explain what you observed, why it matters, and what you recommend changing. If you stopped the run early, explain where and why. Write the review yourself, without AI assistance.

  3. Share your review. Open a GitHub Issue in the assigned student’s Homework 7 repository containing your review. Copy the same review into your Homework 8 submission report and include a link to the GitHub Issue.

The skill has a clear workflow, but the generated report shows that some instructions need clearer definitions and better final checks. 1. The report lists 1.36 and 2.16 parameters for blends, which are incorrect counts. This makes model complexity hard to compare. The skill should explain how to count parameters for each model, including blends. 2. The skill requires one row per candidate and a one-page report. However, the report compares 29 candidates and shows only some of them. Readers therefore cannot check all results. The skill should use fewer tuning values or allow equivalent models to share a row. 3. The findings section exceeds the required 3–5 sentences, and the test error appears twice despite the instruction to report it once. This reduces concision and breaks the reporting rules. The skill should require checking the page length, sentence count, table completeness, parameter counts, and test-error presentation before delivery.
